observations: Photo 0 shows a cross-section of a twin-core cable with stranded copper-colored conductors.
The cable in photo 0 has blue and black inner insulation, a metallic braided shield, and a black outer jacket.
Photo 1 shows two large wooden reels/drums wound with black cable.
No manufacturer markings, brand names, or technical specifications are legible on the cable jacket or the reels.

claims.evidence: The cross-sectional area is not visible in the photos; no markings on the jacket are legible.
The strands are copper-colored, but pure copper cannot be distinguished from copper-clad aluminum (CCA) in a photo.

risks.risk: The cable may be Copper Clad Aluminum (CCA) rather than pure copper, which has lower conductivity.
risks.proof: A close-up photo of a freshly cut strand end to check for a silver/aluminum core.

risks.risk: The gauge (thickness) may be less than the claimed 10mm.
risks.proof: A photo of the printed text on the cable jacket showing the 'mm2' rating.

risks.risk: The cable may not be UV-rated or specifically designed for solar use despite the appearance.
risks.proof: A photo of the jacket printing showing the cable type (e.g., PV1-F).

proof_requests: A clear, close-up photo of the text printed on the cable jacket showing the brand, size (e.g., 2x10mm2), and voltage/standard ratings.
A photo of the label or stencil on the side of the wooden reels.
response.reason: The identity and value of electrical cable depend entirely on the gauge and material (copper vs CCA). Neither can be confirmed without reading the manufacturer's markings on the cable jacket.
